C005.subject: GDP per capita (PPP) in OECD countries
C005.object: material living standards for the bottom 40% of income earners
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita (PPP) in OECD countries material living standards for the bottom 40% of income earners]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Income Distribution Database (IDD) and National Accounts: Compare household disposable income shares for bottom 40% with GDP per capita trends across OECD countries (2000-2023). — Directly tests whether GDP per capita growth diverges from income growth for the bottom 40%, providing cross-country panel data to confirm or refute systematic overestimation.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank's Global Consumption and Income Project (GCIP) microdata: Analyze consumption-based living standards for bottom 40% relative to GDP per capita. — Consumption data better captures material living standards than income, and GCIP offers long-run harmonized microdata to assess the gap with GDP per capita.

[PATH:theoretical] Literature on 'GDP and well-being' (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission, OECD Better Life Index): Review theoretical critiques and empirical studies on GDP per capita as a proxy for median or lower-tail welfare. — Establishes the conceptual framework and prior empirical findings on why GDP per capita may overstate living standards for the bottom 40%, guiding hypothesis refinement.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: material living standards in industrialized economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in industrialized economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and national accounts microdata (e.g., household disposable income, consumption, wealth decomposition) — Directly tests whether GDP per capita diverges from multidimensional measures of material living standards (e.g., median income, consumption bundles, housing quality) in OECD countries post-2000.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative studies of subjective well-being and GDP per capita (e.g., Easterlin Paradox updates, World Happiness Report panel data) — Provides evidence on whether GDP per capita fails to capture perceived material living standards, as subjective well-being often decouples from GDP growth in wealthy economies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical work on 'beyond GDP' indicators (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission, Dasgupta Review on inclusive wealth) — Establishes conceptual frameworks for why GDP per capita omits depreciation of capital, distributional effects, and non-market services, which are critical for material living standards in industrialized contexts.

C007.subject: GDP growth
C007.predicate: increases the prevalence of social comparison anxiety
C007.object: which mediates the negative correlation with subjective wellbeing in post-scarcity societies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth which mediates the negative correlation with subjective wellbeing in post-scarcity societies]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies tracking subjective wellbeing and social comparison anxiety across GDP growth phases in post-scarcity economies (e.g., Nordic countries, Switzerland) — Directly tests whether rising GDP correlates with increased social comparison anxiety and reduced wellbeing, using within-country time-series data to isolate the mechanism beyond the $75,000 threshold.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental studies manipulating relative income salience in virtual economies or laboratory settings with post-scarcity framing — Provides causal evidence for the hypothesized mechanism by inducing social comparison anxiety and measuring its impact on subjective wellbeing, controlling for absolute income levels.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on the Easterlin Paradox and relative income effects in high-income countries — Synthesizes prior findings to assess the consistency of the negative correlation between GDP growth and wellbeing, and the mediating role of social comparison anxiety, identifying gaps and moderators.

qualifier.mechanism: rising relative income concerns beyond the $75,000 threshold

C008.subject: GDP growth
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth subjective wellbeing in post-scarcity societies]

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report longitudinal data (2000-2020) for OECD countries, correlating GDP per capita growth with national average life satisfaction scores — Directly tests the hypothesis by providing time-series data on both GDP growth and subjective wellbeing within the specified temporal and geographic scope, allowing for statistical analysis of correlation strength and direction.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox literature review and meta-analysis (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010; Stevenson & Wolfers, 2008) — Examines the long-standing debate on whether income growth leads to increased wellbeing, particularly in wealthy nations, providing theoretical and empirical context for post-scarcity conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on income shocks and wellbeing in high-income OECD countries (e.g., lottery wins, policy-driven income changes) — Offers causal evidence on the effect of GDP growth (via individual income changes) on subjective wellbeing, helping to address endogeneity concerns in correlational studies.

C011.subject: GDP
C011.object: the economic contribution of unpaid care work by at least 30% in high-income countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP the economic contribution of unpaid care work by at least 30% in high-income countries]

[PATH:empirical] National time-use surveys (e.g., from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Statistics Canada, or Eurostat) combined with replacement cost or opportunity cost valuation methods — These surveys provide direct data on hours spent in unpaid care work. Applying standardized valuation methods (e.g., market replacement cost) allows estimation of the monetary value of unpaid care work as a share of GDP, enabling a direct test of the 30% undercount claim across multiple high-income countries.

[PATH:empirical] Satellite accounts for household production (e.g., those published by the UK Office for National Statistics or the Australian Bureau of Statistics) — These official satellite accounts extend the national accounts framework to include unpaid household services. Comparing the value of unpaid care work captured in these accounts to standard GDP figures provides a rigorous empirical benchmark for assessing the magnitude of the undervaluation claimed in the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on the value of unpaid care work relative to GDP (e.g., OECD reports, academic reviews by the Levy Economics Institute or UN Women) — A systematic review and meta-analysis of published estimates from high-income countries can aggregate evidence across different methodologies and time periods. This would help determine whether the 30% lower bound is consistently supported or refuted, and identify sources of variation (e.g., by country, valuation method, or decade).

C012.subject: GDP
C012.object: essential indicators of economic health and development
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP essential indicators of economic health and development]

[PATH:literature] Stiglitz, J. E., Sen, A., & Fitoussi, J.-P. (2009). Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress. OECD. — This foundational report critically assesses GDP as a measure of economic health and well-being, proposing alternative indicators. It directly challenges the hypothesis by highlighting GDP's limitations in capturing distributional, environmental, and social factors.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank World Development Indicators database: time-series data on GDP per capita, Gini coefficient, life expectancy, and environmental degradation for multiple countries (1990–2023). — Cross-national empirical analysis can test whether GDP growth correlates with improvements in other well-established welfare indicators (e.g., health, inequality, sustainability). Low or negative correlations would refute the hypothesis that GDP captures essential health and development indicators.

[PATH:theoretical] Jones, C. I., & Klenow, P. J. (2016). 'Beyond GDP? Welfare across Countries and Time.' American Economic Review, 106(9), 2426-2457. — This paper develops a welfare-relevant metric that extends GDP by incorporating consumption, leisure, mortality, and inequality. It provides a theoretical framework to evaluate whether GDP alone is sufficient to capture economic well-being, supporting or refuting the hypothesis through formal modeling.
